Receive Channel Messages as a Promise or a Stream

Source: R/promise.R
mizu_recv_async.Rd

mizu_recv_async() returns immediately with a promises::promise() — it never blocks — resolving with the next received payload: the identical R object a blocking mizu_recv() would have returned, zero-copy ALTREP views included. Chain with promises::then() or the promise pipe %...>%.

Usage

mizu_recv_async(ch, timeout = Inf)

mizu_recv_handler(ch, fn, batch = FALSE)

# S3 method for class 'mizu_channel'
as.promise(x)

# S3 method for class 'mizu_channel'
is.promising(x)

Arguments

ch

a channel handle from mizu_channel() (or the ch binding inside a peer expression). Arming a spin channel errors: its publish path skips the wake checkpoint by design.

timeout

seconds after which the promise rejects with the mizu_timeout classed error. Inf (the default) waits indefinitely.

fn

a function(x) called with each received message (or, with batch = TRUE, each burst as one list), and finally with a terminal condition. NULL removes the handler.

batch

deliver each drained burst to fn as one list in a single call, instead of one call per message.

x

for the as.promise method: a channel handle, treated as mizu_recv_async(x).

Value

mizu_recv_async(): a promises::promise() resolving with the next message. mizu_recv_handler(): the channel handle, invisibly.

Details

The promise rejects on mizu_closed, mizu_peer_gone, and on timeout expiry — as classed error conditions carrying the same class names as the sentinels, so inherits(x, "mizu_closed") works on either form. Close and peer death reach the drain through the core's terminal wakes, so the rejection is prompt, never timeout-driven.

Several outstanding calls on one channel resolve in FIFO call order, one message each. Arming is loss-free: messages already in the ring resolve from the arm's synchronous drain (delivered asynchronously at top level, per promises discipline); only genuinely pending entries ride the watch.

mizu_recv_handler() is the stream form: it installs fn on the channel and each burst of messages is delivered to it from the event loop — no promise is allocated per message. With batch = TRUE each drained burst is delivered as one list in a single fn(list) call (the throughput form: one R call per burst); with batch = FALSE, fn(value) is called per message. Transport terminals are delivered to fn as the classed error conditions (mizu_closed, mizu_peer_gone), after which the handler is removed. A declined foreign payload (see mizu_send()) is delivered as its mizu_error_python_payload condition and the handler continues. An error raised by fn removes the handler and propagates at the event loop. mizu_recv_handler(ch, NULL) removes the handler.

A channel holds at most one of the two consumer forms at a time: installing a handler with promises pending, or requesting a promise with a handler installed, is an error. Mixing a blocking mizu_recv() with pending promises consumes in arrival order — the blocking call may take a message a promise was waiting on.

Every main-thread drain is bounded per event-loop quantum and re-scheduled, so a saturated ring starves neither Shiny nor later::run_now().

Requires the later package (and promises for mizu_recv_async()), both of which must be installed.

Examples

if (FALSE) { # interactive() && requireNamespace("promises", quietly = TRUE)
library(promises)
ch <- mizu_channel(quote(mizu_send(ch, mizu_recv(ch))))
mizu_recv_async(ch) %...>% print()
mizu_send(ch, 42L)
later::run_now()
mizu_close(ch)
}
